sections.h2: What sets a Franklin Township, NJ house sale apart from nearby towns?
sections.html:
Franklin Township is a large Somerset County township, and unlike Garfield or Freehold Township it does not require a resale certificate of occupancy for a home sale. The Census Bureau estimates 69,105 residents for July 2025 across 46.17 square miles of land, or about 1,481 people per square mile at the 2020 count.

Housing figures for 2020-2024 show a 69.3% owner-occupied rate, a median home value of $457,900 and median gross rent of $2,115. Median household income is $124,648 and the mean commute to work is 33.5 minutes.

Nearly 35% of residents were born outside the United States, and 40.6% of people over five speak a language other than English at home.

sections.h2: How did the villages and history of Franklin Township shape its housing?
sections.html:
Franklin Township is a collection of villages that grew together over about 280 years. The area was organized around 1745 as the Eastern precinct, and the state recognized the township on February 21, 1798, among the first 104 townships in New Jersey.

The Delaware and Raritan Canal, built in the 1830s, drove early growth, and the old canal towpath is now a state park along the township's northern and western edges. Rockingham, near Kingston, is where George Washington wrote his farewell address to the army in 1783.

Today the named communities include Somerset, Franklin Park, East Franklin, Middlebush, Griggstown, Kingston, Six Mile Run, Pleasant Plains, East Millstone, Blackwells Mills and Weston. In the 2010 census Somerset counted 22,083 people and Franklin Park 13,295, which makes those two the largest. Buyers search by these village names, so use them in your listing or in your conversation with a cash buyer.

sections.h2: Does Franklin Township require a certificate of continued occupancy to sell a home?
sections.html:
No. The township's construction office states that a Certificate of Continued Occupancy inspection is not required when a residential home is sold in Franklin Township. What is required is an inspection from the Fire Prevention Department, reachable at 732-873-2500, extension 6303.

That fire inspection is the state's smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and portable extinguisher compliance check, and the township posts a smoke alarm application among its forms. Commercial sales are different: the township requires a Certificate of Continued Building Compliance for a commercial building or when a new tenant takes the space.

Construction CodeNo resale certificate of occupancy for a residential sale; permits and inspections for open work

sections.h2: What should a Franklin Township owner check about permits and historic districts?
sections.html:
Check two things: whether work on the house was permitted, and whether the property sits in a historic district. The township's permit instructions note that under the Uniform Construction Code, replacing roofs and siding on one- and two-family detached homes no longer requires a construction permit (polypropylene siding is the exception).

That relief does not apply in a historic district. All siding and roof replacements there still need Historic Commission review and approval before work starts, and the township publishes a map of the districts.

  • Look at your last roof, siding, deck and basement jobs and confirm the paperwork exists.
  • Check the township's district map if you plan any exterior repair before selling.
  • Call the Construction Department at 732-873-7283, extension 6224, when you are unsure whether a job needed a permit.

sections.h2: What does Franklin Township require for a vacant or foreclosure property?
sections.html:
The township regulates vacant and abandoned residential properties in foreclosure through Chapter 183 of its code, amended by Ordinance 4393-23, effective March 26, 2023. A mortgagee must inspect after filing a foreclosure complaint and register the property with the Township Clerk within 10 days, with a nonrefundable annual fee capped at $500.

The ordinance matters to a seller because it spells out what happens at transfer. Upon sale or transfer of a covered property, the owner is responsible for all code violations and must meet the Code Enforcement office within 45 days for a final courtesy inspection report. A failure to maintain a covered property can lead to a summons with a fine of up to $1,500.

If you own a house that is headed toward foreclosure, selling before a complaint is filed avoids this registration track altogether. Ask the Clerk's Office whether your address already appears on the vacant property register.

sections.h2: How does the reduced realty transfer fee for seniors apply in Franklin Township?
sections.html:
New Jersey charges a lower realty transfer fee when the seller is a senior citizen, blind or disabled. With Franklin Township's 18.3% share of residents aged 65 or older, this schedule applies to many local sales.

For a price of $350,000 or less, the reduced rates are $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000 and $1.25 per $500 on the portion from $150,000 to $350,000. Above $350,000, the schedule starts at $1.40 per $500 and climbs to $2.65 per $500 for the slice between $550,000 and $850,000.

A seller claiming the reduced schedule files the RTF-1 affidavit with the deed in the Somerset County Clerk's office. Ask your closing attorney to confirm that the seller qualifies before you rely on the lower figure.

A separate GIT/REP residency form travels with the deed as well. The Division of Taxation says the person who signs the deed completes it, and a New Jersey resident uses the GIT/REP-3.

sections.h2: How do schools, highways and parks shape buyer interest in Franklin Township?
sections.html:
Buyers look first at the school district, then at Interstate 287, then at open space. Franklin Township Public Schools serve pre-K through grade 12 across 10 schools, with 7,352 students in 2023-24.

Interstate 287 crosses the northern part of the township with two interchanges, and county routes 514, 518 and 527 carry local traffic. The New Jersey Turnpike lies just outside the township, with its closest interchanges two towns away in Edison, East Brunswick and Monroe.

  • Colonial Park, a 685.5-acre Somerset County park, includes the Arboretum, a rose garden and a golf course.
  • Six Mile Run Reservoir Site, a 3,037-acre state parcel, offers multi-use trails.
  • The Ten Mile Run Greenway covers 684 acres and runs over four miles in length.

The municipality maintains 216.72 of roughly 260 road miles, while Somerset County keeps 34.67 and the state 8.73.

sections.h2: Which sale route fits a Franklin Township seller?
sections.html:
Because Franklin does not ask for a resale certificate of occupancy, the timeline is shorter than in towns that do. The fire inspection and the deed recording are the two fixed steps, and everything else depends on the buyer.

  • A traditional listing works well for a house in good condition when you can wait on a buyer's financing.
  • A private sale suits an owner who already has a buyer and an attorney.
  • A cash offer fits a house with deferred repairs, an estate or a foreclosure notice, as long as the fire inspection is scheduled early.

Call Fire Prevention first, then set the closing date with the buyer's attorney.

faqs.q: Do I need a resale certificate of occupancy in Franklin Township?
faqs.a: No. The township's construction office says a Certificate of Continued Occupancy is not required for a residential sale. You still need the Fire Prevention Department's smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and extinguisher inspection.

faqs.q: Who inspects smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before a Franklin Township sale?
faqs.a: The Fire Prevention Department does. Its number is 732-873-2500, extension 6303, and the township posts a smoke alarm application among its fire prevention forms.

faqs.q: Can I replace my roof before selling without a permit in Franklin Township?
faqs.a: Usually yes for a one- or two-family detached home, since the Uniform Construction Code no longer mandates a permit for roof replacement. A house in a historic district is the exception: it needs Historic Commission approval first.

faqs.q: What is the senior citizen realty transfer fee in New Jersey?
faqs.a: It is a lower schedule for senior citizen, blind or disabled sellers. For prices up to $350,000 it is $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000 and $1.25 per $500 on the portion up to $350,000, claimed on the RTF-1 affidavit.

faqs.q: What happens to a foreclosure property when it sells in Franklin Township?
faqs.a: The owner becomes responsible for all code violations at transfer and must meet the Code Enforcement office within 45 days for a courtesy inspection report. Mortgagees register covered properties with the Township Clerk within 10 days of their inspection.
